reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A benign, hypocellular, myxoid tumour that arises within skeletal muscle, most often in the thigh, shoulder, buttock, and upper arm
It typically presents in middle-aged and older adults, with a female predominance, as a slowly enlarging painless mass
Activating GNAS mutations underlie the tumour, the same gene implicated in fibrous dysplasia
The coexistence of one or more intramuscular myxomas with fibrous dysplasia constitutes Mazabraud syndrome
Histology shows abundant hypovascular myxoid matrix with only scattered bland spindle and stellate cells and no significant atypia
MRI demonstrates a well-defined lesion of low T1 and high T2 signal that behaves almost like fluid, often with a thin rim of surrounding fat and muscle oedema
The cellular myxoma variant is more cellular and vascular and can be mistaken for a myxoid sarcoma
Marginal excision is curative and local recurrence is rare
reference.pathophysiology: Intramuscular myxoma is a benign mesenchymal neoplasm characterised by the production of copious mucoid, hyaluronic acid-rich matrix by scattered fibroblast-like cells. The tumour is driven by post-zygotic activating missense mutations in GNAS, which encodes the alpha subunit of a stimulatory G protein; constitutive signalling through this pathway alters fibroblast behaviour and matrix production. Because the same somatic GNAS mutation can affect skeletal progenitor cells, the lesion shares its molecular basis with fibrous dysplasia, and when the two coexist the combination is termed Mazabraud syndrome. The tumour grows by expansion within the muscle, remaining well demarcated and hypovascular, which accounts for its fluid-like imaging characteristics and its indolent, non-metastasising behaviour. The chief diagnostic challenge is separating it, and especially its more cellular variant, from myxoid soft tissue sarcomas.
additionalInvestigations: MRI to characterise the fluid-like myxoid mass within muscle
Image-guided core biopsy when imaging is not definitive
Histology demonstrating hypocellular myxoid tissue with bland cells
GNAS mutation analysis in equivocal cases
Skeletal survey or targeted imaging for fibrous dysplasia when Mazabraud syndrome is suspected
Correlation of imaging, cellularity, and vascularity to exclude a myxoid sarcoma
redFlags: Increased cellularity, vascularity, or atypia raising concern for a myxoid sarcoma
Bone lesions suggesting associated fibrous dysplasia and Mazabraud syndrome
Recurrence after excision prompting re-evaluation of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Intramuscular myxoma is benign with an excellent prognosis, and marginal excision is generally curative with only rare local recurrence. Recognition of associated fibrous dysplasia in Mazabraud syndrome is important, as those bony lesions carry their own morbidity.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing a myxoid sarcoma from the cellular myxoma variant
Underestimating a hypercellular lesion and missing a genuine myxoid malignancy
Failing to look for fibrous dysplasia and thereby missing Mazabraud syndrome
Attempting enucleation of an ill-defined myxoid mass before imaging characterisation
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Perform marginal surgical excision, which is generally curative with only rare local recurrence
Characterise the lesion with MRI and obtain image-guided core biopsy in equivocal cases to exclude a myxoid sarcoma
Use GNAS mutation analysis to support the diagnosis where imaging and histology are indeterminate
Screen for fibrous dysplasia with a skeletal survey when Mazabraud syndrome is suspected and manage symptomatic bony lesions
Provide routine follow-up after excision given the benign, non-metastasising nature
Review through orthopaedic oncology and pathology multidisciplinary input
